title: Page has exactly one non-empty <title> in the head
why: Google documents the <title> element as the main source of the title link shown in results. Without a non-empty title, Google builds one from other text on the page, which may not describe it well.
fix: Give every indexable page a unique, descriptive <title> in the server-rendered <head>.
thresholds: Fail: 0 non-empty head <title> in the rendered DOM. Warn: missing in raw HTML but present after rendering (see content-title-raw-rendered-mismatch).
notes: In the rendered DOM and the raw HTML, select document.head > title (exclude <title> inside inline <svg>). Fail if it is absent, or if its textContent is empty or whitespace only after trimming and collapsing whitespace. Do not count <title> inside <svg> or <template>. Non-indexable pages (noindex, non-200, canonicalised elsewhere) get info severity only. Lighthouse 13.6 reports the same condition as document-title (SEO and accessibility); do not count it twice.

title: More than one <title> element
why: The HTML standard allows one title element per document. With several, browsers and crawlers use the first, so the others are dead text that may contradict it.
fix: Leave exactly one <title> in <head>. Check the CMS and SEO plugins for duplicate injection.
exemptWhen: The extra <title> elements are inside inline SVG icons, where they are accessible names.
thresholds: Fail: >1 document title elements.
notes: Count <title> elements that are children of <head> in the raw HTML, and count any <title> in <body> outside SVG. Fail if the head count is >1 or a body-level title exists. SVG <title> elements (accessibility names for icons) are legitimate and must be excluded.

title: Title differs between raw HTML and rendered DOM
why: Google renders JavaScript and usually takes the rendered title, but Bing, link-preview bots and most AI fetchers read the server HTML. A placeholder raw title such as the framework default reaches those clients.
fix: Render the final title on the server so every crawler and social scraper sees the same value.
exemptWhen: The title changes intentionally at runtime, for example to show an unread count.
thresholds: Warn when the strings differ after whitespace/case normalisation. Fail when the raw title is empty or a generic placeholder (e.g. 'React App', 'Loading…', the site name only) and only JavaScript sets the real one.
notes: Compare the normalised <title> text in the raw HTML with the rendered DOM after network idle. Google renders JavaScript and generally uses the rendered title. Bing, social previews and LLM fetchers often use the raw HTML. A dynamic title (unread count, A/B test) is a false-positive trap: report the difference, not an error.

title: Identical titles across indexable pages
why: Google documents that identical or near-identical titles across pages make it harder for users to tell results apart and are a common reason for title rewrites.
fix: Make each title describe that page's specific content, e.g. by adding the distinguishing entity, season, product variant or location from the page's h1.
exemptWhen: Paginated pages that are canonicalised or noindex.
Pages that are noindex, non-200 or canonicalised to another page.
Language alternates linked by hreflang that carry the same brand-only title.
thresholds: Medium: any duplicate group. High: ≥10% of indexable crawled pages are in duplicate groups, or the home page title is shared.
notes: Across crawled pages that are 200, indexable and self-canonical, group them by normalised title (lowercase, collapsed whitespace, Unicode NFC). Report groups of size ≥2. Also detect micro-boilerplate: titles identical after removing the brand/site-name segment. Exclude paginated series that differ only by page number when they are canonicalised or noindexed. Exclude hreflang alternates in different languages, which may legitimately share a brand-only title only when the content really is the same. Pages blocked by robots.txt are not seen by Google; report them separately.

title: Title dominated by repeated template text
why: Google lists half-empty titles and titles dominated by repeated site-wide text among the causes of title link rewrites.
fix: Shorten the boilerplate to a concise brand segment at the start or end, separated by a delimiter. Put the page-specific text first.
thresholds: Tool heuristic: warn if uniqueChars < 15 or the template share is >50% of the title's pixel width. Fail if the title equals the site name or '| Site name' only.
notes: Across the site, find the longest common prefix and suffix shared by ≥30% of titles (the template). For each page, compute uniqueChars = length of the title after removing the template parts. Also flag 'half-empty' titles that consist only of a delimiter plus the site name. The thresholds are tool heuristics, not Google figures. Google names 'half-empty' titles and repeated boilerplate as causes of rewrites.

title: Title likely truncated (pixel width), or very short
why: Google sets no length limit on titles and truncates title links to the device width. Very short titles are rewritten more often. Pixel limits used by tools come from industry measurements, not from Google.
fix: Put the most important words first so truncation removes only the brand or secondary words.
thresholds: Info: desktop width >600px ('likely truncated on desktop'). Low: <=20 characters ('short titles are rewritten more often'). No pass/fail. Never claim a Google limit.
notes: Measure the title's rendered width in pixels with a canvas using Arial at 20px (desktop title link) and the mobile equivalent. Count characters too. Google: 'there's no limit on how long a <title> element can be'; it is truncated to the device width. The ~600px desktop figure is industry consensus, not documented by Google. Screaming Frog's measured values (482px desktop, 550px mobile) date from 2014. Zyppy (Q1 2022, 80,959 titles): 61.6% rewritten; lowest rewrite rate at 51–60 characters (39–42%); >60 characters >76%; >70 characters 99.9%. These are correlations with rewrites, not ranking effects. Font metrics differ per script (CJK, Arabic).

title: Keyword-stuffed or list-style title
why: Google cites titles that repeat keywords or list many terms as low quality and a cause of rewrites, and keyword stuffing is a spam policy.
fix: Use one natural descriptive phrase for the page's main topic plus the brand. Drop keyword variants.
exemptWhen: The title contains a product name with model numbers or a breadcrumb-like structure that reads naturally.
thresholds: Candidate: token repeated ≥3 times, or ≥4 separators with average segment ≤3 words. The LLM confirms.
notes: Tokenise the title. Flag it if any non-stopword content token (or its lemma) appears ≥3 times, if there are ≥4 list separators (comma, pipe, slash, middle dot) between short noun phrases with no verb, or if it is a list of place names or phone numbers. Send candidates to the LLM to confirm unnatural repetition. Product names with model numbers or legitimate breadcrumb-like titles ('Shoes / Men / Running') can trip the separator heuristic, so the LLM must judge naturalness. Google cites stuffed titles being shortened.

title: Title and main visible heading disagree
why: Google documents that it may rewrite a title that does not match the main visible heading, or when several headings are equally prominent and none is clearly the main title.
fix: Make the title and the h1 describe the same thing; they need not be identical. Make one heading clearly the main title.
exemptWhen: The home page h1 is a slogan or tagline and the title names the brand and service.
A single h1 combines a keyword line and a tagline (for example in two spans or across a line break); it is one h1.
thresholds: Candidate: Jaccard <0.2 and no shared named entity. The LLM decides whether there is a real topical mismatch.
notes: Find the main heading (the first visible h1 in main content; otherwise the largest-font heading in the first viewport). Compute token overlap (Jaccard on lemmatised content words) between the title (without the brand) and the heading. Send pages with low overlap to the LLM, which decides whether they describe different things. A short h1 with a longer, more descriptive title is fine. Google lists 'no clear main title' (several equally prominent headings) as a cause of rewrites. The home page h1 is often a slogan; the LLM should be lenient there.

title: Title language or script differs from the main content
why: Google documents that it may rewrite a title written in a different language or script from the page content.
fix: Write the title in the same language and writing system as the page's primary content. On multilingual sites, localise titles per language version.
exemptWhen: The title contains brand names, product names or loanwords in another language.
The title has fewer than 4 words, where language detection is unreliable.
thresholds: Fail: both detections confidence ≥0.8 and languages differ. Skip titles under 4 words (detection unreliable).
notes: Detect the language of the title (without the brand) and of the main content text, e.g. with CLD3 or fastText lid, using confidence thresholds. Fail if the languages differ with high confidence, or the scripts differ (e.g. Latin transliteration vs Devanagari content). Brand names, product names and English loanwords in Spanish/Catalan titles are not mismatches. Spanish and Catalan are easily confused by short-text detectors, so require main-content detection to agree with html lang.

title: Year in title is older than the page content
why: Google documents rewriting titles whose year contradicts a newer year on the page, with an example of a title rewritten to match the visible heading.
fix: Update the year in the title only when the content was actually updated for that period. Otherwise remove the year.
exemptWhen: The page is about a historical event or a period identified by that year.
thresholds: Deterministic fail when the title year is older than the h1 year. LLM judgment for 'title says 2023 while content describes current state'.
notes: Extract four-digit years 1990..(currentYear+1) from the title. Compare them with years in the h1/first heading, the visible date and dateModified. Fail if the title's highest year is older than the visible heading year, or older than the dateModified year on a page whose content is clearly time-scoped ('2026 guide', 'admissions 2026'). Historical pages ("1998 World Cup") legitimately carry old years. Google's own example: a '2020 admissions criteria' title rewritten to match a visible '2021' heading.

title: Brand placement and repetition in titles
why: Google may show the site name separately and may drop a repeated brand from the title link. Brand placement is an editorial choice; a missing brand is not an error.
fix: Brand concisely, once, at the start or end, separated by a delimiter (e.g. ' – Brand'). Declare the site name with WebSite structured data on the home page.
thresholds: Low: brand repeated, or brand share >50%. Info: brand absent (Google may show the site name separately).
notes: Using the site name from WebSite JSON-LD name/alternateName, og:site_name or the home page title, check whether it appears in the title. Flag a title where the brand appears more than once, where brand text takes >50% of the width, or where a brand appears mid-title rather than at the start/end with a delimiter. Google may drop a domain-level site name from the title link when it repeats the site name shown in the result. A missing brand is not an error.

title: Exaggerated, shocking or misleading title
why: Google asks whether a title avoids exaggerating or shocking, and its Discover guidance warns against clickbait. Raters treat titles that overpromise relative to the content as low quality.
fix: Make the title describe what the page actually delivers. Remove hype and excess capitals or exclamation marks.
exemptWhen: Marketing copy is persuasive but the content supports the claim.
thresholds: Fail only with quoted evidence of a promise/content mismatch or excessive punctuation/caps hype.
notes: The LLM compares the title and h1 with the main content. Fail if the title promises something the content does not deliver (an unconfirmed release date, a 'best in the WORLD' claim), or uses shock or clickbait framing. It must quote the title and the contradicting or absent content. QRG 5.2 gives low-quality title examples ('Pink Elephant: Part 2 coming soon!'). Marketing pages naturally use persuasive language; flag only deception or exaggeration that the content does not support.

title: No meta description
why: Google builds snippets mainly from page content and uses the meta description when it describes the page better. A missing description never blocks indexing but leaves the snippet to automatic selection.
fix: Write a unique, human-readable summary for key pages first (home page, popular pages). Programmatic descriptions are fine for large database sites if they are diverse and readable.
exemptWhen: The page is noindex, non-200 or canonicalised to another page.
thresholds: Low by default. Medium for the home page and top-level hub pages (click depth ≤1).
notes: Find meta[name=description i] in the head of the raw and rendered HTML. Fail if it is absent or its content is empty. Google builds snippets primarily from page content and uses the meta description only when it describes the page better, so a missing description never blocks indexing. Lighthouse 13.6 reports the same condition as the meta-description SEO audit; do not count it twice.

title: Identical meta descriptions across pages
why: Google documents that identical or similar descriptions on every page are not helpful and recommends a unique description per page.
fix: Use site-level descriptions only on the home page and aggregation pages. Write page-level descriptions elsewhere, starting with critical URLs.
exemptWhen: Pages canonicalised to another page, and paginated pages.
thresholds: Medium: any group ≥2. High: ≥25% of indexable pages share one description.
notes: Group indexable, self-canonical crawled pages by normalised meta description. Report groups of size ≥2, and the share of pages that use the site-wide default description. Google: 'Identical or similar descriptions on every page of a site aren't helpful.' Exclude canonicalised duplicates and paginated pages.

title: Meta description is a keyword list, too short, or not a summary
why: Google gives examples of poor descriptions: keyword lists, the same text everywhere, text that does not summarise the page and very short descriptions. It sets no length limit.
fix: Write one or two sentences that summarise the page and include concrete details, e.g. 'Learn how to cook eggs with this complete guide in 1 hour or less.'
thresholds: Candidate: <8 words, keyword list pattern, equals title, contains '{{', '%s', 'lorem'. The LLM confirms.
notes: Deterministic candidate flags: ≥4 comma-separated short noun phrases with no verb (keyword list), fewer than about 8 words, identical to the title, or contains template placeholders. The LLM then judges whether it summarises this specific page and includes useful specifics (price, author, date, location, hours where relevant). Google gives bad/better examples: keyword list, identical across pages, doesn't summarise, too short ('Mechanical pencil'). There is no length limit; truncation is to device width. Report predicted truncation (desktop ≈920px at 14px Arial, an industry estimate) only as info.

title: data-nosnippet is on unsupported elements, added late by JavaScript, or covers the main content
why: Google honours data-nosnippet only on span, div and section elements. Text inside it is excluded from snippets and from direct input to AI Overviews and AI Mode, so covering the main content has the effect of nosnippet for those surfaces.
fix: Use data-nosnippet only on span, div or section elements. Include it in the server HTML, or when JS first inserts the element.
exemptWhen: The owner deliberately blocks or restricts this crawler or surface; the rule reports the effect as info and never as an error.
thresholds: data-nosnippet on an unsupported element, or added by JavaScript to an existing node = low. data-nosnippet covering most of the main content = medium.
notes: Find elements with the data-nosnippet attribute. Fail if any is not span, div or section. Fail if the attribute appears in the rendered DOM on a node that exists in the raw HTML without it (added by JS). Validate that the containing HTML is well formed (the parser reports no unclosed-tag errors within that subtree). Nodes created entirely by JS that carry the attribute from creation are fine.

title: Large image previews not allowed for articles and Discover-eligible pages
why: Google recommends max-image-preview:large for pages that want large images in Discover, together with images at least 1200 px wide. Google does not document the default when the directive is absent.
fix: Add <meta name="robots" content="max-image-preview:large"> to editorial pages, and provide a representative image at least 1200px wide.
thresholds: Low: absent on article pages. Medium: explicitly 'none' on article pages (unless intentional).
notes: For pages with Article/BlogPosting/NewsArticle JSON-LD or og:type=article, check whether the robots meta allows max-image-preview:large. Flag 'none' and 'standard' explicitly, and report when the directive is absent. Discover recommends images at least 1200px wide, 16:9, and max-image-preview:large. Do not claim what Google's default is when the directive is absent; it is not documented on the page.

title: No main heading (h1) in rendered content
why: Google uses the main visible heading as a clear main title, including when it generates title links. Google states that the number and order of headings do not matter for ranking, so multiple h1 elements are never an error.
fix: Mark the page's main title as an h1 that describes the content.
exemptWhen: A single h1 combines a keyword line and a tagline (for example in two spans or across a line break); it is one h1.
The page has several h1 elements; that is allowed.
thresholds: Medium: 0 visible h1 and no dominant visual title. Info: more than one h1 (allowed).
notes: In the rendered DOM, find visible h1 elements (non-zero box, not display:none or visibility:hidden, not clipped sr-only). Fail if none exists and no element in the first viewport is styled as a dominant title (largest font in main). Report the h1 count as info. Google says the number and order of headings don't matter for ranking. The h1 matters as a clear main title (used for title links) and for accessibility. Never report multiple h1s as an error. The WHATWG spec says a document with headings should have at least one level-1 heading.

title: h1 is empty, hidden, or an image without alt
why: An h1 with no accessible name, or one that is hidden, gives assistive technology and crawlers no main title. An image h1 needs alt text to have a name.
fix: Put the title text in the h1. When a logo image serves as the h1, give it alt text that names the page or brand.
thresholds: Fail: empty accessible name, or every h1 is hidden.
notes: For each h1, compute its accessible name: text content plus alt of contained images plus aria-label. Fail if the name is empty or whitespace, or if the only h1 is hidden (display:none, off-screen, opacity 0). A hidden keyword-laden h1 should also be routed to content-hidden-text.

title: Heading levels skip (accessibility structure)
why: Skipped heading levels make the outline harder to follow with assistive technology. Google states that heading order does not matter for ranking, so this is an accessibility item.
fix: Use heading levels to reflect structure (h2 for sections, h3 for subsections). Style with CSS, not heading level.
exemptWhen: The heading or text belongs to a cookie banner, consent dialog or other overlay outside <main>.
The headings are inside third-party widgets.
thresholds: Low: any skip (e.g. h2→h4). Info only for headings inside third-party widgets.
notes: Walk visible h1–h6 in tree order (respecting the headingoffset attribute if present). Flag each heading whose level is more than 1 greater than the previous heading's level. This is an accessibility and spec-conformance item. Google states that heading order does not matter for ranking. Never present it as an SEO ranking issue.

title: Headings don't summarise their sections
why: Google recommends headings that help users navigate the content and describes clear organisation as helpful for readers and AI systems. It sets no ideal number of headings.
fix: Rewrite headings so a reader scanning only the headings understands the page's outline.
exemptWhen: The heading or text belongs to a cookie banner, consent dialog or other overlay outside <main>.
thresholds: Report a page when ≥30% of its subheadings are generic or non-descriptive, quoting each one.
notes: Extract h2/h3 headings with the text of each section. The LLM judges whether each heading accurately and specifically describes its section. Flag generic headings ('Introduction', 'More info', 'Section 1', 'Click here'), heading text that contradicts its section, and long content (>3 screens) with no subheadings. Google: provide headings to help users navigate; clear organisation helps readers and AI systems. No ideal number of headings.

title: Main content not identifiable (no <main> landmark)
why: Google does not require a <main> element. A single main landmark helps assistive technology and lets this tool separate main content from boilerplate; without it the tool falls back to content extraction.
fix: Wrap the primary content in a single <main> element, keeping header, nav, footer and sidebars outside it.
thresholds: Low: 0 or >1 visible main landmarks.
notes: Count visible <main> or [role=main] elements. Fail if 0 or >1 visible. Report whether an <article> wraps the primary text. Google does not require <main>. Its value is accessibility, and it lets this tool separate main content from boilerplate for the other checks. When it is missing, the tool falls back to a readability-style content extractor.

title: Little unique main content relative to template
why: Google rejects preferred word counts but asks whether a page adds substantial value. Pages where template text dwarfs the unique content are often low value, but many page types are complete with few words.
fix: Make sure each indexable page has substantial content specific to its purpose, or consolidate or noindex thin variants.
exemptWhen: The page is an About, contact or similar page that fulfils its purpose with little text; Google sets no minimum word count.
The page is a product, calculator, gallery or utility page whose purpose needs little text.
The heading or text belongs to a cookie banner, consent dialog or other overlay outside <main>.
thresholds: Candidate only: uniqueMainWords <100 or boilerplate share >80% on non-utility pages. No word-count pass/fail.
notes: Across the crawl, compute DOM text blocks repeated on ≥50% of pages (boilerplate). For each page, compute uniqueMainWords (words in main content not in boilerplate blocks) and the boilerplate share. Send pages whose purpose is informational and that have very little unique text to the LLM to judge whether the main content satisfies the page's purpose. Google explicitly rejects preferred word counts. Product pages, calculators, contact pages and image galleries can be complete with few words. The LLM decides against the page purpose (QRG: amount of MC should fit the purpose).

title: Filler, ads or secondary content push the main content down
why: The rater guidelines describe filler and distracting ads or supplementary content placed before the main content as a poor user experience. Google's page experience guidance asks whether the main content is easy to find.
fix: Put the most helpful content near the top. Move supporting background lower.
exemptWhen: The heading or text belongs to a cookie banner, consent dialog or other overlay outside <main>.
thresholds: Candidate when the first purpose-fulfilling content starts beyond 2 mobile viewports. The LLM confirms with quotes.
notes: The LLM reads the first screenful(s) of rendered main content. It flags pages where low-value filler (long preambles, life stories before a recipe, repeated generic intros) or distracting ads/interstitials push the content that fulfils the page's purpose far down. Deterministic support: character offset of the first paragraph that matches the h1 topic; ad/iframe count above the fold. QRG 5.2.2 'Filler as a Poor User Experience' and 5.3 'Distracting Ads/SC' (Low rating). Supporting content placed lower is acceptable.

title: Content is people-first and adds original value (Google helpful-content self-assessment)
why: Google's guidance on helpful, reliable, people-first content lists questions about originality, effort, expertise and purpose, and warning signs of content made mainly for search engines. Its ranking systems aim to reward content that answers them well. The analyst assesses the page against those questions.
fix: Add first-hand experience, original data or analysis, clear sourcing, and author background. Remove content written mainly for search traffic.
exemptWhen: The page is an About, contact or similar page that fulfils its purpose with little text; Google sets no minimum word count.
The page is a commercial or utility page; it is judged against its purpose, not as an article.
thresholds: High finding when ≥3 search-engine-first warning signs are evidenced, or no original information or analysis beyond the obvious is found on a page whose purpose is informational.
notes: The LLM scores the page against Google's self-assessment questions: content and quality, expertise, people-first, search-engine-first warning signs, and Who/How/Why. Each judgment cites quoted passages. The output is a per-question verdict (yes / no / unclear) with evidence ids, then an overall rating. The helpful content system became part of core ranking in March 2024 and is listed as retired. Do not say a page is 'hit by the helpful content update'. Commercial and utility pages are judged against their purpose, not as articles. Never say a page was hit by an update or penalised. Commodity summaries of widely available facts are a warning sign only on informational pages.

title: Copied, paraphrased or no-added-value main content
why: Google's spam policies and rater guidelines treat main content that is copied or lightly paraphrased without added value as low quality. Licensed and syndicated content is not copying.
fix: Add original analysis, data, media or experience. Canonicalise or attribute syndicated copies. Remove scraped pages.
exemptWhen: The duplicated text is a quotation, a legal text, a licence or manufacturer specifications.
The content is syndicated or licensed and attributed.
thresholds: Candidate: internal shingle overlap ≥80% with another indexable page, or an external exact-match copy found. The LLM decides between Lowest-style (almost all MC copied/paraphrased) and acceptable syndication or licensing.
notes: Deterministic: shingle (5-gram) and SimHash comparison of the main content against other crawled pages. Optional: exact-quote search of 2–3 distinctive sentences via a search API to find external copies. The LLM then judges whether the page adds original content, context or analysis beyond its sources (QRG 4.6.6 and 5.2.1). Licensed or syndicated content (AP, Reuters) is not 'copied' per QRG. Quotes, legal texts and manufacturer specs are expected duplicates. Without an external search API, external copying is not observable; say so. External copying is not observable without a search API; the rule compares pages within the crawl only.

title: Scaled content abuse / doorway pattern
why: Google's scaled content abuse and doorway policies cover many pages generated mainly to rank, whether by AI, people or both, including near-identical pages that only swap a place or keyword and pages built to capture query variants. The rule reports a risk pattern, never a penalty.
fix: Merge into one useful page per real offering, or add genuinely local or unique content (staff, prices, cases, photos per location). Noindex or remove auto-generated variants.
exemptWhen: Location or variant pages carry real per-location or per-variant information.
Language versions are translations linked by hreflang.
thresholds: Candidate: ≥10 pages whose main content differs only by ≤5% of tokens, those tokens being place or keyword substitutions. The LLM must quote ≥2 pages side by side to confirm.
notes: Site-level. Cluster pages by template plus near-identical main content where the only differences are a substituted entity (city, service, product keyword), found by token diff between pages. Also detect pages made of keyword-bearing nonsense. The LLM reviews a sample of ≥3 pages per cluster: do they add unique value, or do they funnel users to the same destination? Applies however the content was made (AI, human, or both). Legitimate location pages with real per-location information are not doorways. Report this as 'risk pattern consistent with the scaled content abuse policy', never as 'penalised'.

title: Leftover AI/template artifacts in published content
why: Google's guidance on generative AI content asks for accuracy and quality whatever the production method. Leftover assistant phrases, template placeholders or unfilled variables show that the content was published without review.
fix: Remove the artifacts and review the whole piece by hand for accuracy; Google asks for manual fact-checking of all AI output, including metadata.
exemptWhen: The site copy discusses AI, agents, prompts or AI products as its subject; only instruction-like text aimed at AI systems placed in hidden text or attributes counts.
The phrase is inside a quotation, a code sample or a blockquote.
thresholds: Fail: any match in main content or metadata.
notes: Regex/phrase scan of the rendered main content, title, meta description and alt text for unedited generation artifacts in en/es/ca, e.g. 'As an AI language model', 'I cannot browse', 'Certainly! Here is', 'Como modelo de lenguaje', 'Com a model de llenguatge', '[insert', '[Your Name]', 'Lorem ipsum', unrendered '{{ }}' or '%s', 'Regenerate response'. Articles that are about AI may quote such phrases legitimately, so require the match outside <blockquote>/<code> and send borderline cases to the LLM.

title: Easily verifiable factual errors or outdated figures
why: Google asks whether content is free of easily verified factual errors, and raters treat inaccurate content as low quality, especially on YMYL topics.
fix: Correct the facts, cite primary sources, and show an updated date when the change is substantive.
thresholds: Report each error with the quote and the reason. Severity escalates to high on YMYL pages.
notes: The LLM lists checkable claims (dates, figures, laws, prices, specs, named facts) and marks those that are internally inconsistent, contradicted by other evidence on the site, or clearly outdated relative to the page date. Optionally verify a sample via web search when the user enables it. Without web verification the LLM may only flag internal contradictions or claims that are dated relative to the page's own dates. It must not assert external facts from its own memory as certain. Planned: without external verification the analyst can flag only internal contradictions and figures dated by the page itself, which is not reliable enough for v1. The analyst must never assert external facts from memory.

title: Spelling and stylistic errors
why: Google lists spelling and stylistic issues among the signs of low effort in its helpful-content questions.
fix: Proofread, especially titles, headings and calls to action.
exemptWhen: The text uses a regional variant, a mix of languages by design, or technical jargon.
thresholds: Low: ≥1 confirmed error per 300 words. Medium: ≥1 per 100 words or errors in title/h1.
notes: Run a language-aware spell/grammar checker (e.g. LanguageTool with the detected language: en, es, ca) on the main content. Exclude proper nouns, code and brand terms. The LLM reviews flagged items and drops false positives. Catalan/Spanish mixing, regional variants (es-ES vs es-MX) and technical jargon cause false positives. The rates are tool heuristics.

title: YMYL classification of the page topic
why: The rater guidelines apply higher standards to topics that can significantly affect health, finances, safety or society. Most topics are not YMYL. The classification sets the context for other judgments.
fix: For YMYL pages, show expert authorship or review, sources, and clear site responsibility.
thresholds: none (classification only)
notes: The LLM classifies the topic as clear YMYL, maybe YMYL, or not YMYL, in the categories Health or Safety, Financial Security, Government/Civics & Society, or Other, and gives the harm rationale. The result raises the scrutiny and severity of E-E-A-T and accuracy findings. Classification only, no pass or fail. Uses title, h1 and main content. The September 2025 rater guidelines updated the YMYL definitions and added government, civics and society. Many or most topics are not YMYL, including most business service sites.

title: E-E-A-T evidence on the page and site (trust first)
why: The rater guidelines describe experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trust, with trust as the most important, and Google's helpful-content guidance asks whether it is clear who created the content. E-E-A-T is not itself a ranking factor.
fix: Publish clear ownership and contact details, author bios with relevant experience, and editorial or review policies. Cite sources.
exemptWhen: A contact section reachable from the footer or navigation as /#contact (or another in-page anchor) counts as a contact page.
thresholds: High: YMYL page with no identifiable responsible entity or author. Medium: non-YMYL commercial page with no clear business identity.
notes: The LLM collects visible evidence of: who is responsible for the site and the content (2.5.2), experience (first-hand detail, original photos), expertise (credentials relevant to the topic), authoritativeness (on-site evidence only, such as cited recognition or client lists with verifiable names), and trust (contact, policies, accuracy, secure transactions). It rates each with quotes and URLs, and marks missing evidence as 'not found on crawled pages'. Trust is the most important part of E-E-A-T, and E-E-A-T is not itself a ranking factor. Reputation information (off-site reviews, news) is not observable from the site; the LLM must not claim a reputation status. Off-site reputation is not observable; the analyst must not claim a reputation status.

title: Hidden text (colour, size, opacity, positioning, behind images)
why: Google's spam policies prohibit text hidden from users but present for search engines, such as text in the background colour, behind images or positioned off screen. They explicitly allow tabs, accordions, sliders, tooltips and screen-reader text.
fix: Remove the hidden text, or make it visible as useful content.
exemptWhen: The content is present in the HTML and has opacity 0 only until an IntersectionObserver reveal (for example [data-reveal]) fires on scroll; Google renders with a tall viewport that triggers it.
The text is in tabs, accordions, sliders, tooltips, menus or screen-reader-only elements.
The heading or text belongs to a cookie banner, consent dialog or other overlay outside <main>.
thresholds: Candidate: hidden text ≥20 words or containing ≥3 repeated target keywords/place names. Critical when the LLM confirms deceptive intent.
notes: In the rendered DOM, for each text node with ≥3 words, compute visibility: font-size <1px, opacity 0, colour contrast ratio against the effective background <1.1:1, positioned off-screen (left/top < -1000px or outside the document scroll area), height 0 with overflow hidden, or covered by an opaque element (elementFromPoint test). Exclude accessible sr-only patterns (clip: rect(0 0 0 0) / clip-path with 1px size and skip links), [hidden] interactive components, accordions/tabs/sliders/tooltips and aria-live regions. The LLM reviews the remaining candidates for keyword-laden content. Google explicitly allows accordion or tabbed content, sliders, tooltips and screen-reader-only text. Consent banners, mega-menus and mobile nav drawers are hidden by design. Report a 'pattern consistent with the hidden text policy', not a penalty.

title: Hidden or disguised links
why: Google's spam policies prohibit links hidden from users, such as a link on a single character or styled to be invisible, when they exist to manipulate ranking.
fix: Remove hidden links. If the site may be compromised, investigate injected code (see content-hacked-signals).
exemptWhen: Icon links with an accessible name, skip links, and links inside closed menus or accordions.
The content is present in the HTML and has opacity 0 only until an IntersectionObserver reveal (for example [data-reveal]) fires on scroll; Google renders with a tall viewport that triggers it.
thresholds: Candidate: any hidden external link. Critical when the LLM confirms it is not a legitimate UI element (icon links with aria-label are legitimate).
notes: For each <a href> in the rendered DOM, flag it if it has zero layout area, an invisible style (same tests as hidden text), anchor text of a single non-alphanumeric character or one letter inside a paragraph, or if it points to an external host and sits inside a hidden container. Group by target host. Icon-only links with an accessible name, skip links, and links inside closed menus or accordions are not abuse.

title: Keyword stuffing in main content
why: Google's spam policies define keyword stuffing as filling a page with keywords or numbers to manipulate ranking, such as lists of cities or repeated phrases out of context. Google publishes no keyword density target.
fix: Rewrite naturally. Replace place lists with real service-area information or a single structured list where users need it.
exemptWhen: Store locators, glossaries and directories list many names or numbers that serve users.
thresholds: Candidates by the heuristics above (tool thresholds, not Google numbers). The LLM must quote the passage.
notes: Detect: (a) blocks listing ≥10 place names or ≥5 phone numbers with little surrounding prose; (b) any 2–4-word n-gram (non-stopword) repeated far above a language baseline, i.e. the same phrase occurring ≥8 times in under 500 words of main content; (c) footer or sidebar keyword lists. The LLM confirms whether the text reads unnaturally. Do not compute or report 'keyword density' targets. Store locators, glossary pages and legitimate directories naturally contain many names or numbers; judge whether there is added value.

title: Different content served to Googlebot user agent (UA-based cloaking)
why: Google's spam policies prohibit cloaking: showing search engines different content from users. The tool compares responses for a crawler user agent and a browser user agent; IP-based cloaking cannot be detected from outside.
fix: Serve the same content to users and crawlers. If the site is compromised, clean up the server and plugins.
exemptWhen: Differences come from bot protection, consent walls, personalisation, ads or tokens.
A paywall shows Google the full content with paywall markup.
thresholds: Fail: main-content SimHash Hamming distance >10, a different title/h1, or new outbound links/keywords present only for the Googlebot UA. Warn: a smaller divergence.
notes: Fetch the URL with a Chrome mobile UA and with the Googlebot Smartphone UA (same IP and headers otherwise), render both, then compare the title, h1, main-content SimHash, outbound link set and redirect target. IP-based cloaking (verified Googlebot IPs) cannot be detected from the tool's IP; say so. Bot-protection challenges, geo/consent walls and personalisation cause benign differences. Paywalls are not cloaking if Google sees the full content and Flexible Sampling is followed. Dynamic rendering that serves equivalent content is not cloaking.

title: Sneaky redirects (device, referrer or UA conditional)
why: Google's spam policies prohibit redirects that send users to a different destination than search engines see, for example only for visitors from search or on mobile.
fix: Remove the conditional redirects. Check for injected scripts if they were not intentional.
exemptWhen: The root URL redirects by country, cookie or language to locale home pages, every locale URL answers 200 when requested directly, and hreflang covers every locale.
Redirects for site moves, consolidations or after login.
thresholds: Fail: final URL registrable domain differs between variants, or a JS redirect to an external domain fires only with a search referrer or a mobile UA.
notes: Load the page in headless Chrome with a desktop UA, a mobile UA, and with Referer=https://www.google.com/. Record HTTP, meta-refresh and JS redirects (navigation events within 10 s of load without user input). Fail if any variant ends on a different registrable domain or an unrelated page, unlike the others. Legitimate: site moves, page consolidation, post-login redirects, and language/region redirects to the same site (these are still bad practice for crawlers, but not sneaky).

title: Back button hijacking
why: Since April 2026 Google's malicious practices policy covers back button hijacking: interfering with browser navigation so that the back button does not return to the previous page.
fix: Remove history manipulation that traps users. Use pushState only on real user navigation (SPA routes, filters).
exemptWhen: A single-page application pushes history entries for navigation the user triggered.
thresholds: Fail: one back action does not return to the previous page.
notes: In headless Chrome: navigate from a blank origin page to the URL, wait 5 s without interaction, then trigger history.back(). Fail if the browser does not return to the origin page (e.g. history.pushState/replaceState injected entries on load, or a popstate handler that navigates elsewhere). Also statically scan scripts for pushState calls at load combined with popstate listeners that navigate. Added to the malicious practices policy on 13 Apr 2026. SPAs that push state on genuine user-triggered navigation are fine; the test must involve no interaction. Hash-based deep-link scrolling that replaces state without adding entries is fine.

title: No signs of hacked or injected content, cloaked spam or injected redirects
why: Google's spam policies cover hacked content: spam pages, links or redirects injected into a site without the owner's consent. Hacked content is often shown only to crawlers, and Google may warn users or remove pages.
fix: Clean the compromise, patch the CMS and plugins, rotate credentials, then request review in Search Console if a manual action exists.
exemptWhen: The site's own topic covers pharmacy, gambling or similar subjects that hacked spam often uses.
thresholds: Critical when ≥1 confirmed injected spam block or URL is found.
notes: Detect off-topic spam vocabulary (pharma, casino, replica, loans, adult, Japanese/Chinese keyword blocks on a non-CJK site) in the main content, hidden blocks or outbound links. Detect unknown external script injections and links to such domains, and pages in the crawl or sitemap unrelated to the site topic (e.g. /wp-content/…/cheap-viagra.html). The LLM checks whether the topics are foreign to the site's purpose. Hacked content may be cloaked (shown only to Googlebot), so run it together with content-cloaking-ua. Legitimate pharmacies and casinos exist; judge relative to the site's own topic.

title: Third-party content exploiting the host's ranking signals
why: Google's site reputation abuse policy covers third-party pages published on a host to benefit from its ranking signals with little first-party oversight. In 2026 Google clarified the policy and its handling in the EEA.
fix: Remove the content, noindex it, or bring it under real editorial control. Keep third-party content clearly related to the site's purpose.
exemptWhen: Press releases, syndicated news, forums, comments, editorial columns and properly disclosed affiliate content.
thresholds: Report as a risk candidate only, with quoted evidence (paths, labels, topic mismatch).
notes: Site level. Find sections whose topic diverges from the site's first-party focus (coupons, casino/loan reviews, 'partner content', 'sponsored', white-label review sections), often under a distinct path or subdomain, sometimes with a different template, byline 'Partner' or identical copies elsewhere. The LLM assesses whether the third-party content appears to lack first-party oversight and to exist mainly to rank. Not violations: press releases, syndicated news, forums and comments, editorial columns, properly handled affiliate content. Since 30 Aug 2026, inside the EEA the manual-action impact does not apply; the section may be separated to rank independently. Outside the EEA the manual action affects the section. Enforcement began 5 May 2024; the policy was clarified 19 Nov 2024 and 21 Jan 2025. Planned: telling third-party sections without first-party oversight from legitimate sections needs signals v1 cannot collect reliably (ownership, editorial process, history).

title: Topic discontinuity suggesting expired domain repurposing
why: Google's expired domain abuse policy covers buying an expired domain to host low-value content that relies on its former reputation. Rebrands and legitimate new owners are common.
fix: If the domain was acquired, build original value for the new purpose. Don't rely on the old site's links or reputation.
thresholds: Info: topic changed. High: change combined with low-value or affiliate content of the kind Google gives as examples (casino on a former school site).
notes: Optional external check: query the Wayback Machine CDX API for the home page across years. Compare the historical topic (title/h1 snapshots) with the current topic. The LLM judges whether the current low-value content exploits a previous unrelated owner's reputation. Google: expired domain abuse 'isn't something people accidentally do.' Rebrands and legitimate new owners are common; never accuse on topic change alone. Planned: needs archived snapshots of earlier versions of the site, which v1 does not collect. Never accuse on a topic change alone.

title: Thin affiliate pages
why: Google's spam policies cover thin affiliate pages that copy merchant descriptions and reviews without adding original value. Affiliate links themselves are fine.
fix: Add original evaluation (evidence, measurements, comparisons). Link to several sellers. Qualify the links with rel=sponsored or nofollow.
thresholds: High when the affiliate page's main content is mostly merchant descriptions without original evaluation (quoted).
notes: Detect affiliate links by known patterns (amazon tag=, amzn.to, awin1.com, tradedoubler, cj.com/anrdoezrs, impact.com/sjv.io, shareasale, partnerize, ?ref=/aff=). For pages with ≥1 affiliate link, the LLM evaluates added value: first-hand testing evidence, comparisons, pros and cons, measurements, multiple sellers (Google's review guidance), versus merchant-copied descriptions. Affiliate links themselves are fine. Copying merchant text without added value is the violation. Merchant text can't be fetched to compare in most cases; the LLM judges from the generic manufacturer-speak style plus evidence.

title: Paid, affiliate or sponsored links without rel=sponsored/nofollow
why: Google asks sites to qualify paid, sponsored and affiliate links with rel=sponsored or rel=nofollow. Unqualified paid links fall under the link spam policy.
fix: Add rel="sponsored" (or nofollow) to paid and affiliate links.
thresholds: Medium: ≥1 such link without a qualifier. High: a sitewide footer or sidebar of unqualified commercial links.
notes: Find outbound links identified as affiliate (patterns above) or inside containers labelled sponsored/advertorial/patrocinado/publicitat/partner. Fail if rel lacks both sponsored and nofollow. Google treats affiliate links 'handled appropriately' as fine; rel=sponsored is the preferred qualifier. Redirect-through-own-domain affiliate links (/go/x) need the redirect to be followed to classify them.

title: User-generated links not qualified and UGC spam
why: Google recommends rel=ugc or rel=nofollow for links in user-generated content and documents how unmoderated UGC spam affects a site.
fix: Add rel=ugc or nofollow to user links, moderate comments, and use anti-spam measures.
thresholds: Medium: unqualified UGC outbound links. High: confirmed spam posts in UGC.
notes: Locate UGC regions (comments, forum posts, reviews, profiles via common markup/classes, Comment/DiscussionForumPosting schema). Flag outbound links there without rel=ugc or nofollow. The LLM flags spammy UGC (off-topic commercial links, gibberish, repeated promotional posts). Google updated its UGC spam guide on 26 Oct 2026 to help platforms detect spam earlier.

title: Visible link scheme patterns
why: Google's link spam policy covers link exchanges, keyword-rich links in widgets or footers across sites, and other links meant to manipulate ranking. Only outbound links on the audited site are observable.
fix: Remove the links or qualify them with rel=sponsored/nofollow. Drop link-exchange pages.
exemptWhen: A design or development credit in the footer, or an agency linking to its own clients.
thresholds: High when the LLM confirms followed, keyword-anchored, unrelated sitewide links or link-exchange pages.
notes: Detect sitewide (≥50% of pages) footer, sidebar or template outbound links to unrelated commercial sites with keyword-rich anchors, 'partner'/'link exchange' pages listing reciprocal links, low-quality directory listings, and widget-embedded links. The LLM judges relevance and likely payment. 'Web design by Agency' footer credits are common; flag them only if keyword-stuffed and followed across many client sites (an agency's own site linking to clients is normal). Inbound link schemes are not observable.

title: Links with no accessible anchor text
why: Google uses anchor text to understand the linked page, and an image's alt text serves as anchor text for image links. Links with no text and no alt give no context.
fix: Add descriptive text. For image links, set alt to describe the destination.
thresholds: Medium: any empty-anchor internal link. Low: external.
notes: For each <a href>, compute its anchor text: text content, plus alt of child images, plus aria-label/aria-labelledby, with title as a fallback. Fail if empty. Google uses an image's alt as anchor text and title as a fallback for empty links. aria-label helps accessibility, but Google does not document it as an anchor text source; report the Google signal separately.

title: Anchor text is descriptive, concise and not stuffed
why: Google recommends descriptive anchor text that is reasonably concise, and lists generic anchors such as "click here" and very long or keyword-stuffed anchors as poor practice.
fix: Use concise, descriptive anchors that make sense out of context, e.g. 'pricing for logo design' instead of 'click here'.
thresholds: Low: generic anchors in main content (report the count and examples). Low: >100 characters. Medium: stuffed/repeated exact-match anchors.
notes: Compare normalised anchor text against a multilingual generic list (en: click here, read more, here, more, link, website, article; es: haz clic aquí, aquí, leer más, más información, ver más; ca: clica aquí, aquí, llegir més, més informació). Flag anchors longer than 100 characters or full sentences, chained adjacent links, and identical keyword-rich anchors repeated to the same internal target ≥10 times per page. 'Read more' in card grids next to a descriptive heading link is common; downgrade to info when the same target already has a descriptive link nearby. The 100-character threshold is a tool heuristic (Google: 'weirdly long'). Lighthouse 13.6 reports generic anchors as the link-text SEO audit; do not count it twice.

title: Sources cited and outbound link policy
why: Google notes that linking to sources can help users verify claims and build trust, and advises nofollow only for links the site does not vouch for.
fix: Cite primary sources with descriptive anchors. Use nofollow only for untrusted links.
thresholds: Low: all editorial external links nofollow. Medium: YMYL page with ≥3 unsourced statistical claims.
notes: Deterministic: count in-content external links and the share with nofollow. Flag a site where 100% of external editorial links are nofollow. The LLM flags factual or statistical claims (numbers, studies, 'according to') that cite no source on informational or YMYL pages. Google: linking to sources can build trust; use nofollow only when you don't trust the source. Links to own social profiles are not citations.

title: Content images have an alt attribute
why: Google uses alt text, together with computer vision and the surrounding text, to understand images, and alt text serves as anchor text for linked images. A missing alt attribute leaves no text alternative; an empty alt is correct for decorative images.
fix: Add alt text that describes the image in the page's context. Use alt="" only for purely decorative images.
exemptWhen: The image has alt="" and is decorative (a logo next to the text name, an illustration, a divider); an empty alt is correct markup for decorative images.
Tracking pixels and spacer images.
thresholds: Counts images with no alt attribute at all. Medium: a content image (inside main, at least 100x100 CSS px, not aria-hidden or role=presentation) without an alt attribute. Low: other images without an alt attribute. alt="" is never counted as missing.
notes: For each (and input type=image) in the rendered DOM, fail if the alt attribute is absent. Separately count alt="" (valid for decorative images). For inline

title: Low-quality alt text (stuffed, filename, generic)
why: Google recommends alt text that describes the image in context and warns against keyword stuffing in alt attributes.
fix: Write short, information-rich descriptions, e.g. 'Dalmatian puppy playing fetch' rather than 'puppy dog pup puppies'.
exemptWhen: The image has alt="" and is decorative (a logo next to the text name, an illustration, a divider); an empty alt is correct markup for decorative images.
thresholds: Low per issue type. Medium when keyword-stuffed alts appear sitewide.
notes: Flag alt values equal to the filename or matching camera/hash patterns (IMG_\d+, DSC\d+, [a-f0-9]{16,}), a generic single word ('image', 'photo', 'imagen', 'foto', 'imatge', 'logo' on a non-logo image), lists of ≥4 comma-separated keywords, the same alt repeated on ≥5 different images on a page, or alt >250 characters. The LLM checks a sample for relevance to the image and page. Google gives no alt length limit; the 250-character threshold is a tool heuristic. Functional images in links should describe the destination (WAI).

title: Non-descriptive image filenames
why: Google describes descriptive filenames as a very light clue about an image's subject. Hashed names from a CMS or CDN are common and low impact.
fix: Use short, descriptive, localised filenames, e.g. my-new-black-kitten.jpg, URL-encoding non-Latin characters.
thresholds: Low: ≥50% of content images on a page have opaque names.
notes: Parse the basename of each content image src. Flag generic or opaque names: image\d*, img\d*, IMG_\d+, DSC_?\d+, screenshot-\d+, untitled, or a pure hash/UUID. Exclude CDN-transformed URLs where the original name is preserved in the path. Many CMSs and CDNs hash filenames; Google calls filenames a light signal ('very light clues'). Keep this low severity.

title: Important images delivered only as CSS backgrounds
why: Google documents that it does not index images referenced only in CSS and extracts images from img elements. Hero, product and editorial images delivered as CSS backgrounds are not eligible for Google Images.
fix: Use (or ) with src and alt for images that should appear in Google Images or convey content.
exemptWhen: The background is decorative, such as a texture or gradient.
thresholds: Medium: hero, product or editorial image only as CSS background. Info: decorative backgrounds.
notes: Find elements in main content or above the fold with a computed background-image url() whose area is ≥40% of the viewport width, and the Lighthouse LCP element when it is a background image. Fail if there is no / equivalent of the same visual on the page. Google doesn't index CSS background images and extracts images only from img src (clarified 16 Apr 2024). Decorative textures are fine as backgrounds.

title: Unsupported image format or extension/type mismatch
why: Google Images indexes BMP, GIF, JPEG, PNG, WebP, SVG and AVIF. Images in other formats without a supported fallback are not indexed.
fix: Serve a supported format, e.g. AVIF/WebP with a JPEG/PNG fallback in the img src.
exemptWhen: A <picture> element offers an unsupported format with a supported img fallback.
thresholds: Medium: unsupported format with no supported fallback in <picture>. Low: extension mismatch.
notes: For each content image, fetch its headers and sniff the bytes. Fail if the format is not one of BMP, GIF, JPEG, PNG, WebP, SVG or AVIF (e.g. HEIC, TIFF, JPEG XL as the only source). Warn if the URL extension disagrees with the actual type. AVIF support was added on 30 Aug 2024. <picture><source type=image/jxl> with an img src JPEG fallback is fine.

title: Content images load without user interaction
why: Google documents that Googlebot does not scroll or click, but renders with a tall viewport, so images that load when they enter the viewport are found. Images that load only after a scroll event or a click are not.
fix: Remove loading=lazy from above-the-fold images. Use native lazy-loading or IntersectionObserver, which load without user actions.
exemptWhen: The content is present in the HTML and has opacity 0 only until an IntersectionObserver reveal (for example [data-reveal]) fires on scroll; Google renders with a tall viewport that triggers it.
Images use loading="lazy" or an IntersectionObserver and load in a tall-viewport render.
thresholds: Medium: LCP image lazy-loaded, or content images never resolved without user scroll.
notes: Flag loading=lazy on the LCP image or on images intersecting the initial mobile viewport. Flag images whose real URL is only in data-src/data-srcset with a placeholder src that is not swapped in the rendered DOM without scrolling (render with a tall viewport, no scroll, then compare). Google Search does not interact with pages (no scrolling or clicking); Googlebot uses a tall viewport, so IntersectionObserver-based loading generally works.

title: Representative preferred image (og:image / primaryImageOfPage)
why: Google documents og:image and primaryImageOfPage as ways to indicate the preferred image for a page, and recommends large images for Discover.
fix: Specify a relevant, high-quality image per page via primaryImageOfPage or og:image, not the logo. Use ≥1200px wide, 16:9, for Discover.
exemptWhen: Several pages share one Open Graph image; unique og:image values are not required.
The image is an SVG, so its pixel size cannot be measured: the size check is not_evaluated, never failed.
thresholds: Low: missing or logo on content pages. Medium: unreachable image. Info: <1200px wide (Discover).
notes: Check for og:image and/or schema.org primaryImageOfPage (or an image on the mainEntity). Fail if absent on article and product pages, if it points to the site logo (URL or alt contains 'logo', or it is the same image on ≥50% of pages), if it is <1200px wide on editorial pages, or if it is unreachable (non-200 or blocked by robots). Preferred-image guidance was added on 2 Mar 2026. Reference each image with one consistent URL (12 May 2025 clarification).

title: Video watch pages: embed, thumbnail and VideoObject
why: Google indexes videos as video results only on watch pages, where the video is the main content, and recommends VideoObject markup with a reachable thumbnail.
fix: Add VideoObject markup with a stable thumbnail. Make the video the page's main content. Consider a video sitemap.
exemptWhen: The video supports an article rather than being the main content of the page.
thresholds: Medium: watch page missing VideoObject or with an unreachable thumbnail. Info: blog posts with embedded video (not watch pages).
notes: For pages whose main purpose is a single video (one dominant <video>/<iframe> player in main): check that the player is in the rendered HTML and not hidden; that VideoObject JSON-LD has name, description, thumbnailUrl and uploadDate; that the thumbnail URL returns 200, is ≥60×30 and is not robots-blocked; and that name and description are unique. Since the Aug 2024 overhaul, only watch pages are indexed as video results; supporting videos in articles aren't. A VideoObject 'creator' property was added on 24 Sep 2026.

title: Byline, author page and Person markup
why: Google's helpful-content guidance asks whether it is clear who wrote content where one would expect it, and its article markup documents author properties that should match the visible byline.
fix: Show who wrote each article, link to an author page with relevant background, and mirror it in Article markup.
exemptWhen: The content is published under the organisation's name.
thresholds: Medium: article without a visible byline where one is expected, or markup author not matching the visible byline. Low: no author page or url/sameAs. Low: author.name contains extra text.
notes: For article-like pages (Article/BlogPosting/NewsArticle schema, og:type=article, or a /blog/ path with a date), detect a visible byline (rel=author, [itemprop=author], a 'By/Por/Per' pattern near the h1). Check that the byline links to an author page with a bio. Check that JSON-LD author is Person/Organization, that author.name contains only the name (no 'by', job title, or multiple names merged), that author.url or sameAs is present, and that the markup names match the visible byline. Bylines are expected 'where one might be expected': not on product pages, service pages or the home page. Organization authorship is valid. Fake author personas or AI headshots are a deception signal (people-first guidance).

title: Visible dates match structured data and sitemap lastmod
why: Google recommends a visible publication or update date that matches datePublished and dateModified in structured data, and uses these to show dates in results. AI search features also use dates for freshness.
fix: Show one clearly labelled date, match it in datePublished/dateModified, include a timezone, and minimise other dates near the byline.
exemptWhen: The visible dates are event dates rather than publication dates.
thresholds: Medium: visible vs structured mismatch, or a future date. Low: lastmod differs from dateModified by >1 day. Low: missing labels ('Published'/'Updated').
notes: Extract the visible published/updated dates near the byline (with locale-aware parsing for en/es/ca month names) and JSON-LD datePublished/dateModified (ISO 8601). Fail if they disagree (calendar date), if any date is in the future, if dateModified < datePublished, or if the timezone is missing when a time is given. Compare the sitemap lastmod with dateModified. Event pages show event dates; those are not publication dates (Google: use Event markup). Time and timezone may appear only in structured data.

title: Dates bumped without substantive changes
why: Google lists changing page dates to look fresh without substantial changes as a warning sign of search-engine-first content.
fix: Update dates only when the content changes substantively. Generate dateModified from real content revisions.
exemptWhen: The change is template-wide (footer, navigation) and dates were not updated.
thresholds: Medium: sitewide identical or per-request dateModified. Medium: date changed with <2% content change between runs.
notes: Site level. Flag when dateModified (or the visible 'Updated' date) equals the crawl date or one shared date on ≥80% of pages, or is generated per request. When historical snapshots exist (previous tool runs), compare main-content SimHash: dateModified changed but content distance <2% means a cosmetic update. The people-first guidance lists 'changing the date of pages to make them seem fresh when the content has not substantially changed' as a warning sign. Template-wide changes (new footer) are not content changes.

title: About and contact information are easy to find
why: The rater guidelines treat clear information about who runs a site and how to contact them as part of trust, with the amount expected depending on the site's purpose, and more for shops and YMYL topics.
fix: Link About, Contact and policy pages from the footer. On the about page, state who runs the site, with location and contact channels.
exemptWhen: A contact section reachable from the footer or navigation as /#contact (or another in-page anchor) counts as a contact page.
The page is an About, contact or similar page that fulfils its purpose with little text; Google sets no minimum word count.
thresholds: Medium: no about or no contact page reachable within 1 click. High: e-commerce or YMYL site with no contact or returns information.
notes: From the home page and footer links, look for: About (about, nosotros, quiénes somos, qui som, sobre nosaltres), Contact (contact, contacto, contacte) with a physical address, phone or email, and Privacy and legal pages (privacy/privacidad/privadesa, aviso legal/avís legal, terms, cookies). For e-commerce, also look for returns/refunds and shipping. The LLM checks that the about page identifies a real responsible entity. QRG 2.5.2/2.5.3 and 4.5.1 (inadequate information for the page's purpose). The amount needed depends on purpose: a hobby blog needs little, a shop or YMYL site needs a lot. In the EU, legal-notice pages are often legally required, but that is outside SEO scope.

title: Stale content signals on time-sensitive pages
why: Google uses freshness systems where users expect recent information. Evergreen content does not need frequent updates, and Google warns against cosmetic date changes.
fix: Refresh outdated facts and figures and update the date accordingly, or label the content as historical.
thresholds: Candidate thresholds as above (tool heuristics). The LLM confirms that freshness matters for the topic.
notes: Deterministic candidates: a year in the title/h1/URL older than currentYear-1 on non-historical topics; a visible updated date older than 24 months on pages with prices, software versions, laws or rankings; phrases like 'this year (2022)' or 'as of 2023'. The LLM judges whether the topic deserves freshness and quotes the outdated statements. Evergreen content does not need frequent updates (Google warns against cosmetic freshness). Freshness systems apply where users expect fresh content (QRG 18.0 'Needs Met Rating and Freshness').

title: Topical focus signals (title, h1, intro, URL, anchors)
why: Google understands synonyms and does not require exact phrases, but a page whose title and main heading never name its topic is harder to understand. No keyword density is computed.
fix: Make the main topic explicit in the title, the main heading and the opening, and use descriptive internal anchors to the page.
thresholds: Info, with one low-severity flag: the topic is absent from both the title and the h1.
notes: Derive the page's primary topic phrase: the LLM proposes it from the title and h1, or the user supplies a target query. Deterministically report whether the phrase or its close variants appear in the title, the h1, the first 100 words of main content, the URL slug (localised), the alt of the main image, and the anchors of internal links pointing to the page (from the crawl graph). Report entity mentions (named entities in the main content). Output an alignment table, not a score. No keyword density. Google understands synonyms and doesn't require exact phrases or long-tail variants (AI optimization guide). Keywords in domain or URL have 'hardly any effect' beyond breadcrumbs.

title: Search intent match
why: The rater guidelines grade how well a result meets the needs behind a query. Without a target query from the owner the analyst infers one and says so.
fix: Align the page format with the intent (a guide for Know, a tool or product page for Do, location info for Visit-in-person). Answer the core need early.
thresholds: High: likely 'Slightly Meets' or 'Fails to Meet' for the stated target query.
notes: Given the target query (user-supplied, or inferred from the title/h1 and labelled as inferred), the LLM classifies the dominant intent (Know/Know Simple, Do, Website, Visit-in-person, multiple) per QRG 12.7. It judges whether the page type and content satisfy that intent (Needs Met scale vocabulary: Fully/Highly/Moderately/Slightly/Fails) and quotes the passages that satisfy or fail it. Without SERP data the LLM cannot know what currently ranks; it judges intent fit from the query semantics. State the assumption when the query is inferred. Without search result data the analyst cannot know what ranks; it judges intent fit from the query semantics only.

title: Coverage and depth versus the user's need
why: Google asks whether content provides a substantial, complete description of the topic. Completeness depends on purpose and no word count is recommended.
fix: Add the missing core information. Don't pad with tangential subtopics.
thresholds: Medium: ≥2 core needs missing.
notes: The LLM lists the questions a searcher with the identified intent would reasonably need answered. It marks which are answered (quoting them), missing, or superficial, and whether the page leaves users needing to search again. Comprehensiveness depends on purpose; not every page should be long. Don't recommend word counts.

title: Language-aware readability and wall-of-text
why: Google does not use reading-level scores, but long paragraphs and sentences make content harder to use. Reported as user-experience context only, in the page's language.
fix: Break long paragraphs, add subheadings, and shorten very long sentences, matching the target audience.
thresholds: Info: scores. Low: ≥3 paragraphs >150 words, or p90 sentence length >40 words (tool heuristics).
notes: Detect the language. Compute sentence and paragraph statistics for all languages: mean and p90 sentence length in words, paragraphs >150 words, and sections >400 words without a subheading. Formula by language: English uses Flesch Reading Ease (206.835 − 1.015·words/sentence − 84.6·syllables/word). Spanish uses Szigriszt-Pazos perspicuity (206.835 − 62.3·syllables/word − words/sentence) interpreted on the INFLESZ scale (<40 very difficult, 40–55 fairly difficult, 55–65 normal, 65–80 fairly easy, >80 very easy), with Fernández-Huerta optional. Catalan has no validated formula: report the statistics only. Use language-specific syllabification. Readability is not a ranking factor (Mueller 2018: Google doesn't use basic reading-level algorithms). Report it as UX only. Legal or technical audiences legitimately need complex text. Do not apply English Flesch to Spanish or Catalan. Formulas such as Flesch are language-specific; no score is computed for languages without a validated formula.
